subject: gdistsamp Offset vs no Offset Abundance and Density

messages.author: 8e9d5025a45e12b7
messages.subject: gdistsamp Offset vs no Offset Abundance and Density
parts:
Hello,

I had a question about offsets and how to implement them in gdistsamp. I'm using gdistsamp to calculate the density of a species. I conducted 100m radius PCs (binned every 10m for Unmarked) and 12 sites 7 times throughout the summer. Currently in the example I'm going to show, all 100m radius point counts in this example are treated as having equal area. Just for context there are experimental treatments I included in the phiformula model for each of these. 

area <- pi*100^2/10000

I decided to run a model calculating density without using an offset given this conversation: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/offset%7Csort:date/unmarked/SAKKFOYnO3A/vLBCcBdrCgAJ as it was mentioned that "The output="density" option includes the area offset automatically." 

This is the model and first row from predicted density results from that. 

i1 <- gdistsamp(lambdaformula= ~Treatment, phiformula= ~1, pformula = ~1, keyfun="hazard", output="density",unitsOut="ha", se=TRUE,K=50, data = df)
newdata_trtdense <- data.frame(Treatment= as.factor(c("A", "B", "C")))
predict_dense<-predict(i1, type="lambda", newdata=newdata_trtdense, appedData=T)  
predict_dense$Playback<-paste(newdata_trtdense$Playback)  

i1 - density without offset
Treatment      Predicted         SE               lower          upper
      A             1.867042     0.6251729    0.9685719   3.598953

I figured the predicted value must represent 1.867042 birds/total area in hectares (1.86/ha is too high). So I thought if I divided it by the area, I would get the appropriate density I wanted which is 0.5945994/ha. (This seems closer to reality). 

I also thought that calculating the abundance should give me the same thing if that's what the output of the density was. However, abundance gave me the following result:

i2 <- gdistsamp(lambdaformula= ~Treatment, phiformula= ~1, pformula = ~1, keyfun="hazard", output="abund", se=TRUE,K=50, data = df)
newdata_trtabund <- data.frame(Treatment= as.factor(c("A", "B", "C")))
predict_abund<-predict(i2, type="lambda", newdata=newdata_trtabund, appedData=T)  
predict_abund$Playback<-paste(newdata_trtabund$Playback) 


i2 - abundance without offset
Treatment      Predicted         SE               lower          upper
      A            1.058828      0.5286693    0.3979453   2.817264


Dividing the predicted value by the area this time gives me a density of 0.3370354, not the same as my density results

Just out of curiosity I wanted to see what would happen with an offset for area included since I realized I'm unsure as to what output I'm receiving. I ran both density and abundance models again with the only difference this time being the inclusion of the log(offset(area)) in lambda.

i3 <- gdistsamp(lambdaformula= ~Treatment, phiformula= ~1+log(offset(area)), pformula = ~1, keyfun="hazard", output="density",unitsOut="ha", se=TRUE,K=50, data = df)
newdata_trtdenseoff <- data.frame(Treatment= as.factor(c("A", "B", "C")))
predict_denseoff<-predict(i3, type="lambda", newdata=newdata_trtdenseoff, appedData=T)  
predict_denseoff$Playback<-paste(newdata_trtdenseoff$Playback)  


i3 - density with offset
Treatment      Predicted         SE               lower          upper
      A             0.3272650   0.1647852    0.1219834   0.8780079


i4 <- gdistsamp(lambdaformula= ~Treatment, phiformula= ~1+log(offset(area)), pformula = ~1, keyfun="hazard", output="abund", se=TRUE,K=50, data = df)
newdata_trtabundoff <- data.frame(Treatment= as.factor(c("A", "B", "C")))
predict_abundoff<-predict(i4, type="lambda", newdata=newdata_trtabundoff, appedData=T)  
predict_abundoff$Playback<-paste(newdata_trtabundoff$Playback)   

i4 - abundance with offset
Treatment      Predicted         SE               lower          upper
      A             1.028057     0.5176523    0.3831916   2.758153



i3 is equal to i4 divided by the area. That makes sense and it seems like including the offset is the way to go. 

However I suppose I'm a little confused as to what my outputs are and I have a few questions:

1) Since the output="density" option includes the area offset automatically, what is the reason for the different results between i1 and i3/why does i1 have such a large number? i3 seems a lot closer to correct when considering the #birds that I was aware of in these plots and considering the abundance output. 

2) Since the abundance is the amount of birds per site area (so here 100m radius), why does adding an offset change the values? Does abundance behave differently than density in terms of needing to define the area?

3) What is the offset/lack of offset doing to the results in each of these contexts and what is the correct practice (i.e. is it prudent to always include the offset whether the area is constant or not, or are there situations where you might not want to include an offset for area/size of site)?


I hope the above is clear and that my questions make sense. 

I greatly appreciate any insight that you have. 


Much appreciated.


Stephen

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: gdistsamp Offset vs no Offset Abundance and Density
parts:
An offset is not specific to unmarked.  If you type ?offset in R:

"An offset is a term to be added to a linear predictor... with known coefficient 1 rather than an estimated coefficient."

It makes sense for a Poisson regression when the rate (lambda) is thought to scale with time or space.  But the key is that you log-transform the units (e.g., minutes, hours, area) such that:

E(N) = lambda = exp(beta0 + offset(log(area)))

which is the same as

E(N) = lambda = exp(beta0 + 1*log(area))

which is the same as

E(N) = lambda = exp(beta0)*area

For each equation, beta0 is the log-scale abundance for area = 1 unit.  You don't need to use an offset if all the areas are the same for each survey (e.g., point counts) because you can simply do the math afterward.  Alternatively, if you use output="density" in distsamp or gdistsamp, the abundance estimate (log-scale) is relative to your units specified, either "ha" or "kmsq", instead of being specific to the plot size.  An offset is helpful/necessary when the sizes of your survey plots differ across the study.

It seems Stephen was making a critical mistake in that his offsets were specified for the phiformula, not the lambdaformula (he also incorrectly had a log-transform of the offset, instead of an offset of the log-transform).  Using an offset for probabilities is not recommended, as there is not the same theoretical justification for a probability scaling with time/space as with a Poisson rate.

Finally, understanding how these models work takes more than just reading this listserve or the help files.  Aside from the primary literature, Marc and Andy's "Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology" is the go-to source for getting the most out of unmarked.  The best way to learn is to simulate data and see how well/poorly the simulated values are estimated.  Trying to interpret model output based on your inclinations about the observed data or study sites is not a great way to learn these models, as perceptions can often lead you astray.  Better to learn the models through examples and simulations before unleashing on your own data.
